newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Dostum loses Afghan province to mutineers.
newsitem.headline: Dostum loses Afghan province to mutineers.

text.p: Northern Afghan militia leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum lost control of a northwestern province to mutineers on Monday, but held onto his stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif, a Pakistan-based news service said.

"Dostum's forces appear to have brought the situation under control in Mazar-i-Sharif this (Monday) afternoon," the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said, adding that troops loyal to dissident General Abdul Malik had taken over Faryab province to the west.
AIP said Malik's forces had launched the mutiny early on Monday in four northern provinces, Faryab, Samangan, Jowzjan and Balkh, the capital of which is Mazar-i-Sharif.
It said Malik, a brother of Rasul Pahlivan, a powerful Dostum commander assassinated in Mazar-i-Sharif last year, had switched loyalties to the purist Islamic Taleban militia.
The Taleban, who control the Afghan capital Kabul and more than two thirds of the country, have been trying to oust Dostum and other opposition leaders from northern provinces.
Witnesses in Maimana, capital of Faryab province, said portraits of Dostum had been removed and white flags were flying from government buildings to signify support for the Taleban.
AIP said Faryab province was in Malik's hands, but had no immediate word on the situation in Samangan or Jowzjan.

It cited some reports as saying that former Herat provincial governor Ismail Khan, who has been fighting the Taleban in northwest Afghanistan, had been arrested by Malik's forces along with eight of his men, but there was no immediate confirmation.

Aid workers contacted in Mazar-i-Sharif, 300 km (187 miles) northwest of Kabul, said the city was calm, but rumours were flying. They had no reports of fighting in the town itself. AIP said Dostum's troops had clashed with mutineers in one area.

U.N. officials in Islamabad said Dostum's security officers at Mazar-i-Sharif airport had asked the United Nations not to send any planes there between midday and 4:00 p.m. (0730 and 1130 GMT) for unexplained security reasons.
Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, was a key commander for the pro-communist government led by president Najibullah, who was hanged by the Taleban when they captured Kabul on September 27.
He formed a loose alliance with two other leaders after the fall of the capital and their forces have been locked in combat with the Taleban north of Kabul and in northwest Afghanistan.

In April 1992 he switched sides to support mujahideen guerrilla groups which had battled Soviet troops occupying Afghanistan in the 1980s. Dostum's backing enabled the mujahideen to take over Kabul from Najibullah.
In January 1994 he allied with Hezb-i-Islami leader Gulbuddin Hekmatyar to stage an abortive coup attempt in the Afghan capital against then-president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

Dostum was given the defence ministry in a new government formed by Rabbani in Mazar-i-Sharif earlier this month, but no post was announced for Ahmad Shah Masood, Rabbani's former military chief and a key member of the anti-Taleban alliance.
